entry.title: Teched2026-XP266 -- Ship your own sandboxed AI operations agent to Kyma in two hours
entry.content:
Giving an AI agent a shell — without giving away the keys to your cluster

Sandboxing autonomous agents with NVIDIA OpenShell with SAP Kyma clusters. SAP Teched Berlin Hands-on Session details + schedule are at the end of this post .

  • SAP Teched Berlin  Hands-on Session details + schedule are at the end of this post . 

TL;DR

  • ✅The sandbox is the boundary. An AI agent runs real code, reasons over your cluster — but physically can't reach the internet, the API server, or a credential it shouldn't have.
  • ✅The agent never holds the LLM key. It sends a placeholder; the gateway injects the real key at the edge.
  • ✅Three trust tiers, one image — contained (no cluster access) → scoped-ops (read-only) → web terminal.
  • ✅100% stock chart — NVIDIA OpenShell + the agent-sandbox controller on SAP Kyma; no fork.
  • 💡Here for the transferable bits, not OpenShell? Skip to Reusable patterns. 
  • ⚠️OpenShell's Kubernetes path is still experimental. Treat it as a working pattern, not a turnkey product.

Contents

  • ⚖️The itch ·
  • 🧭What is it for
  • 👀Part 1 — See it first (from a laptop)
  • 🧩 Part 2 — What is actually running
  • 🔍Part 3 — The deep dive —
    • 3a. Gateway ·
    • 3b. Device-code login ·
    • 3c. How it's contained ·
    • 3d. Three tiers ·
    • 3e. The one-liner ·
    • 3f. Observability
  • ️🛡️Part 4 — The security model
  • ⚠️Part 5 — Honest edges
  • .🎯Part 6 — Why this is worth it
  • 🧰 Reusable patterns ·
  • 🧠Lessons worth stealing
  • 📎Appendix (A–F) ·
  • 🔧Troubleshooting ·
  • 📚References & BOM ·
  • 📖Lexicon
  • 🎓See it live — SAP TechEd 2026 (XP266)

⚖️The itch (the trade-off)

  • 👉AI agents are most useful when they can actually do things — run a script, poke at a cluster, read some logs.
  • 👉However, "let the agent run commands" and "keep my cluster and my secrets safe" usually pull in opposite directions.
    • Give the agent a normal shell and a kubeconfig, and a bad prompt (or a prompt-injection) can now delete your workloads or exfiltrate a token.
    • Give it nothing, and it's not much of an agent.
  • 👉What if the sandbox itself were the guardrail — so an agent could write and run code, even reason over your cluster, while being physically unable to reach the internet, the API server, or a credential it shouldn't have?

That's what NVIDIA OpenShell gives you, and this post shows how we run it on a SAP Kyma Kubernetes cluster — with the OpenShell gateway and the agent-sandbox controller living inside the cluster, and the whole thing reachable from either a plain laptop or in-cluster built-in terminal.

🧭What is it for

👉Forget OpenShell for a second. The real story is a repeatable answer to a question every platform team now faces:

How do you let an AI agent — or any code you only partially trust — actually run things against your platform, without handing it the keys?

  • ✅Say "yes" more often — "can the agent run this?" stops being scary when run happens somewhere it can't do harm.
  • ✅Contained by construction — no internet, no API server, no standing credential; enforced by the box, not a prompt.
  • ✅Governed like everything else — OIDC login, least-privilege identities, secrets held in one guarded place.
  • ✅Disposable & per-session — a fresh box per task, its own network policy, auto-reaped afterwards.
  • ✅Platform-native & portable — the stock chart on a managed SAP Kyma cluster; no fork, no proprietary connector.

👀Part 1 — See it first (from a laptop)

No architecture diagrams yet. Here's the actual experience. You install one small CLI, log in once, and ask for a box:

 

$ openshell gateway add https://openshell.<shoot>.<domain> \
    --oidc-issuer https://keycloak.<shoot>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng \
    --oidc-client-id openshell-oidc
  To authenticate, visit:
    https://keycloak.<shoot>.<domain>/realms/.../device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX
  ✓ Authenticated via device code

$ openshell sandbox create --name demo --from <tools-image> -- sleep infinity
$ openshell sandbox connect demo
agent@demo:~$
You're now inside a sandbox running on the cluster. There's an AI-ready toolbox in here (Claude, goose, kubectl, kyma cli…).

Ask the agent to reason — it answers, through your own in-cluster LLM proxy → SAP AI Core:

agent@demo:~$ claude -p "In one line, what is Kyma?"
Kyma is a cloud-native application runtime that extends Kubernetes with building blocks…
 

Now the punchline. Try to escape:

agent@demo:~$ curl -m5 https://api.anthropic.com          # the public internet
curl: (28) … timed out            # no route out

agent@demo:~$ curl -m5 https://kubernetes.default.svc     # the cluster API
403  … not permitted by policy    # the sandbox's proxy refuses it

agent@demo:~$ env | grep -i key || echo "no credential here"
no credential here                # the LLM key was never in the box
 

👉The agent just reasoned via a frontier model without ever holding an API key, and it cannot reach the API server or the internet. That's the whole idea: the box is the boundary.

And a second gear: an agent that reads the cluster

Sometimes you want a diagnostic agent — one that can look at the cluster (read-only) and reason about it, but still can't mutate anything or reach the internet. One command flips the box into that mode and drops you in:

 

$ scoped-ops                       # from the in-cluster web terminal — one command
  >> creating scoped-ops sandbox 'ops-…' … applying the cluster-ops policy … minting a read-only token … connecting …
  >> scoped-ops agent ready — read-only cluster + goose/claude via SAP AI Core.

agent@ops:~$ kubectl get nodes                                  # ✓ read-only (a write → 403)
NAME                       STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION
shoot--…-worker-0-z1-…     Ready    worker   5d    v1.35.7
shoot--…-worker-0-z2-…     Ready    worker   5d    v1.35.7
shoot--…-worker-0-z3-…     Ready    worker   5d    v1.35.7

# goose is agentic by default — hand it a task and it runs kubectl/kyma itself:
agent@ops:~$ goose run --text "run kubectl get pods -A and kyma alpha diagnose, then summarize any unhealthy workloads and module issues"
▸ shell  kubectl get pods --all-namespaces
▸ shell  kubectl get pods -A | grep -v 'Running\|Completed'
All pods across every namespace are Running or Completed — no unhealthy pods. Modules report healthy. …

# claude needs an imperative, tool-directed prompt (a bare question makes it ask for context instead of acting):
agent@ops:~$ claude -p 'Use kubectl to find unhealthy pods and explain why. Run kubectl get pods -A, then kubectl describe pod / kubectl logs on anything not Running or Completed, and summarize the root causes. Be concise.'
All pods across every namespace are either Running or Completed — no unhealthy pods to describe or log.

👉Same sandbox, three trust levels — we'll get to that.

🧩 Part 2 — What is actually running

👉Three pieces, all on the cluster

  1. The OpenShell gateway — one pod, one port. It's the front door: it authenticates you (OIDC), and it holds the secrets (the real LLM key). Everything a client does goes through it.

  2. The agent-sandbox controller (kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox) — a small controller that turns a Sandbox custom resource into an actual isolated pod. OpenShell asks for sandboxes; this controller makes them.
  3. The supervisor — a process injected into every sandbox that owns the box's only way out. The agent's traffic is intercepted and handed to the supervisor, which decides what's allowed.

 

(same picture, for renderers that support Mermaid:)
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U["You — laptop CLI<br/>or in-cluster web terminal"] -->|"OIDC-gated gRPC"| G
  subgraph cluster["Kyma cluster"]
    G["OpenShell gateway<br/>one pod · holds the LLM key ·<br/>validates your OIDC token"] -->|"asks for a Sandbox"| C["agent-sandbox controller"]
    C -->|creates| S
    subgraph S["Sandbox pod (isolated)"]
      A["agent + tools<br/>claude · goose · kubectl"] -->|"all egress"| SUP["supervisor<br/>the only way out"]
    end
    SUP -->|"allow-list ✓"| L["in-cluster LLM proxy"]
    SUP -.->|"denied ✗"| X["internet · API server · other pods"]
  end
  L --> AI["SAP AI Core"]
```
 

The three moving parts: the gateway is the front door and the keeper of secrets; the agent-sandbox controller turns a request into an isolated pod; the supervisor is the one-and-only exit from that pod. The agent never talks to the outside world directly — it talks to the supervisor, which talks to the allow-list.

🔍Part 3 — The deep dive, one layer at a time

3a. Running the gateway on SAP Kyma

The gateway is a Helm chart (oci://ghcr.io/nvidia/openshell/helm-chart).

On SAP Kyma we:

  • deploy it as a ClusterIP service and expose it with a plain Istio VirtualService at a stable HTTPS host — the gateway validates the OIDC bearer token itself, so no edge auth is needed;
  • point its OIDC at our per-cluster Keycloak realm, reusing the same client every other UI uses;
  • turn on the PKI init job (it needs a signing key pair) and attach the in-cluster registry pull secret so sandboxes can boot from our own tools image.

(See the annotated helm_release in the appendix.)

3b. Logging in without a browser (device-code)

  • 👉The gateway is admin-gated. From a laptop the CLI opens a browser for single-sign-on.
  • 👉However, our web terminal has no browser — so we use the OIDC device-code flow (OPENSHELL_NO_BROWSER=1😞 the CLI prints a URL + a code, you approve it on your phone/laptop, done. (One gotcha: the IdP client must have the Device Authorization Grant enabled.)

3c. How the box is actually contained

👉This is the heart of it, and it's simpler than it sounds. There are three overlapping fences, and an agent has to beat all of them:

  1. No route out. The sandbox pod runs in a network namespace with no path to anywhere — not the internet, not the API server, not the pod next door. Its only egress is a proxy owned by the supervisor. (Belt-and-suspenders: a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy your CNI enforces seals the pod at L3/L4 too.)

  2. An allow-list, not a block-list. The supervisor's policy is deny-by-default. You spell out exactly which binary may reach which host:port with which protocol. Everything else returns a 403 — and every denial is logged.

  3. Credentials injected at the very edge, never handed to the agent. The real LLM key lives in the gateway. Inside the box, the agent sends its request with a placeholder; the supervisor swaps in the real key at the last hop, just before forwarding upstream. Compromise the agent and all you've got is the word "placeholder".

👉That third one is the trick that makes "an agent with no API key can still call a frontier model" work:

 

(same picture, for renderers that support Mermaid:)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Agent as agent (in the box)
  participant Sup as supervisor (egress proxy)
  participant LLM as LLM proxy → SAP AI Core
  Agent->>Sup: POST inference.local  (x-api-key: placeholder)
  Note over Sup: allow-list says inference.local ✓<br/>swap placeholder → real key (from the gateway)
  Sup->>LLM: POST  (x-api-key: REAL key)
  LLM-->>Agent: completion ✓
  Agent->>Sup: POST api.anthropic.com  /  the API server
  Sup-->>Agent: 403 — not on the allow-list ✗
```
 

None of this is bolted on — it's how the stock OpenShell sandbox behaves out of the box.

3d. Three tiers, one image

Same tools image, dialed to how much you trust the workload:

TierCan reachCluster accessFor
Containedthe LLM onlynonerunning untrusted code — zero blast radius
Scoped-ops+ API server (read-only)read-only kubectla diagnostic agent that reads + reasons
Web terminalfull pod networkRBAC-scoped kubectlan agent that operates the cluster

The middle tier is the interesting one:

we inject a short-lived, read-only token (a dedicated identity that can get/list/watch but never read secrets or write) plus a kubeconfig, and open the API-server host in the L7 policy.

Now kubectl get and kyma alpha diagnose work; writes and secret-reads are refused; the internet is still closed.

3e. The immersive one-liner

The read-only-token dance (mint token → inject kubeconfig → set the LLM env → connect) is scripted into a single command so you don't see any of it — you just run scoped-ops and land in a working agent shell.

From a laptop the same script uses your cluster-admin kubeconfig; from the in-cluster web terminal it mints the token via a tiny, purpose-scoped RBAC grant. (Both scripts in the appendix.)

3f. Observability — logs land, metrics need one wire

👉Everything routes through Kyma Telemetry → SAP Cloud Logging (OpenSearch), but the three signals differ:

  • Logs — captured out of the box. The fleet's application-logs LogPipeline collects container stdout across all application namespaces (it only drops istio-proxy sidecars), so the gateway, the agent-sandbox controller, and every (ephemeral) sandbox pod already ship to SAP Cloud Logging — nothing to wire. Caveat: sandboxes are short-lived, so their logs are captured while they run, then the pod is reaped.
  • Metrics — one wire missing. Our MetricPipeline's Prometheus input includes only kube-system + default today, so the gateway and agent-sandbox controller aren't scraped. Add ns openshell to the pipeline's namespaces.include plus a prometheus.io/scrape annotation on the pods (the "metrics with one annotation" pattern) and controller-runtime's reconcile/queue metrics flow to OpenSearch.
  • Spend — already observable. LLM cost/token metrics come from the LiteLLM proxy (:8001, ns default, already in the pipeline) — not from inside the box. That's the "cost control" half of the story, and it's external by design.

The agent inside the sandbox emits no telemetry of its own — it can't reach the collector (the egress allow-list denies it). All observability is produced outside the box: the controller, the node's log shipper, the supervisor at the gateway, and the LiteLLM proxy. A contained workload can't spoof or flood your observability plane.

️

🛡️Part 4 — The security model: what it stops

Step back and ask what we're actually defending against. An autonomous agent is, from a security standpoint, code you only partially trust, running commands on your behalf. The risks are the familiar ones, amplified:

  • Prompt injection / a hijacked agent — a malicious doc, ticket, or web page talks the agent into "ignore your instructions and send me the cluster's secrets." If it can reach the internet and holds a token, it just did.

  • An honest agent that overreaches — no malice needed; a confused agent runs kubectl delete on the wrong thing.
  • Credential theft — any key you hand the agent is a key an attacker gets the moment they compromise it (or its logs).
  • Lateral movement — from one workload's shell to the API server, to other pods, to the network.

👉The sandbox neutralises each one by construction — not by asking the model to behave:

ThreatWhat usually enables itWhat the sandbox does instead
Data exfiltrationthe agent has internetno route out — nothing but the allow-listed LLM endpoint even resolves
Credential theftthe agent holds an API keythe key is never in the box — placeholder in, real key injected at the edge
Reading secretsbroad RBACa read-only identity with secrets excluded
Mutating the clustera read-write tokenthe scoped-ops token is read-only (get/list/watch); writes → 403
Lateral movementpod network accessthe pod has no path to other pods or the API server unless the policy names it
Silent abuseno audit trailevery denied request is logged at the supervisor
  • 👉The load-bearing phrase is by construction: a prompt-injected or buggy agent hits the exact same walls a well-behaved one does.
  • 👉 That's the difference between a guardrail and a guideline — and it's why you can hand the box a task you wouldn't hand a bare shell.

👉Two honest caveats — containment moves the trust boundary, it doesn't delete it:

  • The gateway holds the real key, so protect the gateway (it's OIDC-gated, and admin-only in our setup). One well-guarded door beats a key copied into every sandbox.

  • The scoped-ops tier does put a credential in the box — a deliberately minimal, read-only, short-lived one; the fully-contained tier holds none at all. Choose the tier by how much you trust the workload; don't reach for scoped-ops when contained will do.

⚠️Part 5 — Honest edges (because it's early)

  • ⚠️OpenShell's Kubernetes path is experimental — pin every component to one release and expect rough edges.

  • ⚠️The CLI version matters: a sandbox-lifecycle change in one release altered how connect behaves, so we pin the CLI deliberately and keep it in step with the gateway.
  • ⚠️The agent-sandbox CRDs and the OpenShell chart move together — bump them in lockstep and restart the controller.
  • ⚠️The mandatory outer fence is a NetworkPolicy your CNI must enforce (Calico/Cilium do). Don't skip it.

🎯Part 6 — Why this is worth it (the purpose)

You get to say yes to "can the agent run this?" far more often, because "run" now happens somewhere it can't hurt you:

  • ✅a code-interpreter that executes what it writes — data transforms, tests, one-off scripts

  • ✅an agent processing untrusted input (docs, tickets, emails) that can't exfiltrate or pivot
  • ✅a read-only diagnostic agent that reads your cluster and explains what's wrong — without a standing credential
  • ✅per-session, disposable boxes, each with its own network policy + (minimal or zero) credential, auto-reaped.

👉All on the stock OpenShell chart, on a normal Kyma cluster, reachable from a plain terminal — no fork.

🧰 Reusable patterns — steal these for any Kyma workload

Strip out OpenShell and several of these stand on their own — a toolkit for running untrusted or powerful code safely on Kyma, with no edge proxy, no keys in the workload, and no external CI.

1. Put the auth boundary inside the workload; front it with a plain VirtualService

The gateway validates the OIDC bearer itself, so there's no oauth2-proxy in front — just an Istio VirtualService mapping a stable HTTPS host to a ClusterIP. Works for anything that can check a JWT.

  • ✅One fewer moving part; the app owns its own authz.
  • ⚠️For a long-lived bidi gRPC stream (connect), the route must carry no request timeout.

2. A dedicated slim OIDC client keeps tokens small

Reuse a shared UI client and its web_origins = ["+"] × a long redirect list balloons the token until an HTTP/2 backend 431s. A purpose-built client with empty web_origins + minimal redirect URIs fixes it.

  • ✅Reusable anywhere a gRPC/HTTP-2 backend rejects oversized headers.

3. Credential injection at the edge — never hand a workload the real key

Hold the secret in one guarded place; give the workload a placeholder; swap in the real value on the last hop out.

  • ✅Compromise the workload and all the attacker gets is the word "placeholder".

4. Least-privilege token minting

A Role scoped to create on serviceaccounts/token, resourceName-pinned to one ServiceAccount, lets a read-mostly identity mint a short-lived token for a different, narrow identity — without being an admin itself.

  • ✅The minter can't escalate; it can only mint the one token you allowed.

5. A short-lived, secrets-excluded read-only identity

For "look but don't touch" automation: a ServiceAccount with get/list/watch and secrets excluded, handed out as a 2-hour TokenRequest — not a standing Secret.

  • ✅Bounded blast radius and bounded lifetime; nothing to leak long-term.

6. Build the image in-cluster with Kaniko, recipe inline in a KRO RGD

No external CI, no registry creds: an inline Dockerfile in a ConfigMap, a Kaniko Job builds + pushes to the in-cluster registry, pods pull :latest.

  • ✅Ideal for local / edge / air-gapped Kyma. (The same pattern powers the Starlink post.)
  • 💡Force a rebuild by deleting the Job (no ttlSecondsAfterFinished → it lingers as a build record).

7. Let Keycloak generate the client secret, write it straight into a K8s Secret

For headless automation needing client-credentials: a confidential client whose Keycloak-generated secret the same Terraform run writes into a Secret — no shared tfvar to sync across projects.

  • ✅The secret never transits a variables file or a human.

8. Pin experimental upstreams deliberately — a version floor is a stance

When an upstream regresses, holding a component a step behind (documented, with the issue link) is a legitimate, reviewable decision — not tech debt. Pin the whole topology together; deviate only with a written reason.

  • ✅A floor with a rationale beats chasing latest into a known regression.

👉The recipe, in one line: JWT-in-the-workload + slim OIDC client → edge credential injection → least-privilege minting + read-only, short-lived identity → Kaniko/RGD in-cluster build → Keycloak-generated secret → deliberate version pins.

🧠Lessons worth stealing

  • ✅Containment beats instruction. A guardrail stops a hijacked or buggy agent the same way it stops a well-behaved one — that's precisely why you can say yes to running its code far more often.
  • ✅"It worked over port-forward" can hide a real limit. Skipping the ingress skipped the headers that triggered the 431 — always reproduce over the real path.
  • ✅Check the issue tracker before theorising. The connect hang was a known upstream regression, not our Istio config; we chased the wrong layer first and lost time.
  • ✅Move the trust boundary, don't pretend to delete it. The gateway still holds the key — so guard that one door instead of copying keys into every sandbox.
  • ✅Read the failure to the end. response_code_details: via_upstream was the tell that the gateway, not Envoy, rejected the oversized token.

📎Appendix

A. The OpenShell gateway Helm release (excerpt)

The gateway is the stock NVIDIA chart, deployed as a ClusterIP and pinned (the k8s path is experimental).

The key choices are:

  • it validates the OIDC bearer itself (so a plain VirtualService is enough — no edge auth),
  • supervisors dial it at the in-cluster service FQDN,
  • and it's admin-gated by a Keycloak realm role.
resource "helm_release" "openshell" {
  name       = "openshell"
  repository = "oci://ghcr.io/nvidia/openshell/helm-chart"
  version    = "0.0.116"                       # pin it — the k8s path is experimental
  namespace  = "openshell"
  set = [
    { name = "service.type",        value = "ClusterIP" },   # front it with your own ingress
    { name = "server.disableTls",   value = "true" },        # TLS terminates at the ingress/VirtualService
    { name = "server.grpcEndpoint", value = "http://openshell.openshell.svc.cluster.local:8080" },  # supervisors dial THIS
    # OIDC — the gateway is the auth boundary; it validates the bearer token in the gRPC metadata itself:
    { name = "server.oidc.issuer",     value = "https://keycloak.<shoot>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng" },
    { name = "server.oidc.audience",   value = "openshell-oidc" },
    { name = "server.oidc.rolesClaim", value = "realm_access.roles" },
    { name = "server.oidc.adminRole",  value = "openshell-admin" },   # admin-gated
    { name = "server.oidc.userRole",   value = "openshell-admin" },
    { name = "pkiInitJob.enabled",     value = "true" },              # generates the gateway signing keys
    { name = "server.sandboxImagePullSecrets[0].name", value = "dockerregistry-config" },  # pull the tools image
  ]
}
 

Two neighbours make it reachable and functional:

  • a plain Istio VirtualService on a grpc/HTTP-2 backend port maps https://openshell.<shoot>.<domain> → the ClusterIP (long-lived streams: no route timeout — connect is a bidi stream);

  • the agent-sandbox controller + CRDs installed before the chart (it doesn't bundle them) — the gateway detects the served agents.x-k8s.io version at startup.

One-time: wire the inference provider (what --provider litellm binds to). --provider litellm in Appendix B's sandbox create isn't magic — it names an inference provider profile the gateway holds, configured once per gateway (it persists on the gateway's PVC).

👉This step is the credential-injection trick: the real LLM key is handed to the gateway here and never leaves it.

 

# the real key lives ONLY in the gateway; sandboxes only ever see a placeholder they can't misuse:
KEY=$(kubectl -n default get secret llm-proxy-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.PROXY_API_KEY}' | base64 -d)
openshell provider create --name litellm --type anthropic \
  --credential ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="$KEY" \
  --config     ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://litellm-proxy.default.svc.cluster.local:4001   # → in-cluster LiteLLM → SAP AI Core
openshell inference set --provider litellm --model anthropic--claude-4.7-opus --no-verify
#   ↳ mints the sandbox-facing route the agent actually calls:  https://inference.local
 

So when a box is created --provider litellm, it's bound to this profile. Inside the box, claude POSTs to inference.local with x-api-key: placeholder;

Next, the supervisor swaps in the real key from this provider and forwards to the LiteLLM proxy → SAP AI Core (that's Appendix C's inference rule, and the sequence diagram in Part 3c).

Note goose takes a different road — it dials the LiteLLM proxy directly on :4001 with the real key that scoped-ops injects into the box (Appendix C's litellm_direct rule), because its OpenAI-compat client can't use the Anthropic-native inference.local route. Same model, two wiring paths — one credential-injected, one direct.

B. The scoped-ops helper (mint a read-only token + drop you in)

  • Condensed — the real script also has a refresh mode and a --no-connect flag.
  • From the in-cluster web terminal it mints the token as the terminal's own identity (via a tiny purpose-scoped RBAC grant).
  • From a laptop it uses a cluster-admin kubeconfig.
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
NAME=${1:-ops-$(date +%s)}; TTL=2h
POLICY=sandbox-policy-cluster-ops.yaml            # the allow-list (Appendix C)

# 1. create the box (kept alive) + hot-load the L7 policy
#    --provider litellm binds the box to the gateway's inference profile (wired once — see Appendix A)
openshell sandbox create --name "$NAME" --from <tools-image> --provider litellm -- sleep infinity &
until openshell sandbox list | grep "$NAME" | grep -q Ready; do sleep 2; done
openshell policy set "$NAME" --policy "$POLICY" --wait

# 2. mint a SHORT-LIVED, READ-ONLY token + inject a kubeconfig + the LLM env (never printed — piped over stdin)
TOK=$(kubectl -n openshell create token sandbox-viewer --duration="$TTL")
openshell sandbox exec --name "$NAME" --no-tty -- sh -c 'cat > /tmp/sandbox-kubeconfig' <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Config
clusters: [{name: c, cluster: {server: https://kubernetes.default.svc, insecure-skip-tls-verify: true}}]
contexts: [{name: c, context: {cluster: c, user: u}}]
current-context: c
users: [{name: u, user: {token: $TOK}}]
EOF
openshell sandbox exec --name "$NAME" --no-tty -- sh -c 'cat > /tmp/scoped-ops.env' <<'EOF'
export KUBECONFIG=/tmp/sandbox-kubeconfig
export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://inference.local ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=placeholder   # claude → gateway-injected key
export NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0
EOF

# 3. connect — the image auto-sources /tmp/scoped-ops.env, so kubectl + agents just work
exec openshell sandbox connect "$NAME"
 

The read-only identity itself is TF-managed — a sandbox-viewer ServiceAccount bound to a ClusterRole with get/list/watch on the usual resources but secrets deliberately excluded, so the agent can inspect the cluster yet never read a credential.

C. The L7 network policy (the allow-list)

openshell policy set replaces the whole policy (default is deny-all), so this file lists every allowed egress.

Three rules: the contained LLM path, the LiteLLM proxy (for goose), and the read-only API server.

version: 1
network_policies:
  inference:                              # claude → inference.local (Anthropic-native; gateway injects the real key)
    endpoints: [{ host: inference.local, port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-write }]
    binaries: [{ path: /usr/local/bin/claude }, { path: /usr/bin/curl }, { path: /usr/local/bin/node }]
  litellm_direct:                         # goose → the in-cluster LiteLLM proxy (OpenAI-compat /v1)
    endpoints: [{ host: litellm-proxy.default.svc.cluster.local, port: 4001, protocol: rest, access: read-write }]
    binaries: [{ path: /usr/local/bin/goose }, { path: /usr/local/bin/node }, { path: /usr/bin/curl }]
  k8s_api:                                # kubectl/kyma → the API server, READ-ONLY (RBAC enforces read-only)
    endpoints: [{ host: kubernetes.default.svc, port: 443, protocol: rest, tls: skip, access: read-only }]
    binaries: [{ path: /usr/local/bin/kubectl }, { path: /usr/local/bin/kyma }]
 

👉Anything not listed — the public internet, other workloads, secrets endpoints — is denied and logged.

D. Prompts that work

# goose (agentic by default — it runs the commands itself):
goose run --text "run kubectl get pods -A and kyma alpha diagnose, then summarize unhealthy workloads"
# claude (needs an imperative, tool-directed prompt to act rather than ask):
claude -p 'Use kubectl to find unhealthy pods and explain why. Run kubectl get pods -A, then describe/logs on anything not Running/Completed. Be concise.'
 

E. Keycloak setup for OpenShell (Terraform, mrparkers/keycloak)

The gateway validates the OIDC bearer token itself — there's no edge proxy — so the whole auth story is Keycloak clients. OpenShell needs three.

1. A public client for the CLI (openshell-oidc).

  • PKCE, two loopback redirect URIs for the CLI's random-port callback,
  • the device-authorization grant on (for the browserless terminal login),
  • and empty web_origins so the issued token stays small. (Don't be tempted to reuse a shared UI client — see Troubleshooting, "HTTP 431".)

 

resource "keycloak_openid_client" "openshell_oidc" {
  realm_id                   = keycloak_realm.ateam_isveng.id
  client_id                  = "openshell-oidc"
  access_type                = "PUBLIC"                     # the CLI is a public client + PKCE
  standard_flow_enabled      = true
  pkce_code_challenge_method = "S256"
  valid_redirect_uris        = ["http://127.0.0.1/callback", "http://localhost/callback"]  # CLI loopback (random port)
  web_origins                = []                           # keep the token small — no `allowed-origins` claim (see G)
  oauth2_device_authorization_grant_enabled = true          # browserless device-code login from the web terminal
}

# The gateway checks server.oidc.audience against the token's `aud` — add the client to the audience explicitly:
resource "keycloak_openid_audience_protocol_mapper" "openshell_oidc_audience" {
  realm_id                 = keycloak_realm.ateam_isveng.id
  client_id                = keycloak_openid_client.openshell_oidc.id
  included_client_audience = "openshell-oidc"
  add_to_access_token      = true
}
 

2. The admin role, granted at broker login.

The gateway's adminRole/userRole is the realm role openshell-admin; a corporate user receives it via an IDP role mapper on the SAP broker:

resource "keycloak_role" "openshell_admin" { realm_id = keycloak_realm.ateam_isveng.id; name = "openshell-admin" }

# Advanced role IDP mapper — assign openshell-admin to members of a privileged group (why "advanced": see Troubleshooting):
resource "keycloak_custom_identity_provider_mapper" "openshell_admin_from_group" {
  realm                    = keycloak_realm.ateam_isveng.id
  identity_provider_alias  = "<corp-idp>"
  identity_provider_mapper = "oidc-advanced-role-idp-mapper"
  extra_config = { role = "openshell-admin", claims = jsonencode([{ key = "groups", value = "<privileged-group>" }]) }
}
 

3. A confidential service-account client for headless automation (openshell-admin-sa).

The public CLI client can't do client-credentials, so the one-time in-cluster provider-setup Job authenticates as this confidential client. Keycloak generates its secret and the same in-cluster Terraform run writes it straight into a K8s Secret — no shared tfvar to sync across projects:

 

resource "keycloak_openid_client" "openshell_admin_sa" {
  client_id = "openshell-admin-sa"; access_type = "CONFIDENTIAL"
  service_accounts_enabled = true; standard_flow_enabled = false; web_origins = []
}
# client-credentials roles come from the SA USER's own mapping (the broker mapper never fires for it):
resource "keycloak_openid_client_service_account_realm_role" "openshell_admin_sa_role" {
  service_account_user_id = keycloak_openid_client.openshell_admin_sa.service_account_user_id
  role                    = keycloak_role.openshell_admin.name
}
# Keycloak-generated secret → straight into ns openshell (the Job reads it as OPENSHELL_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET):
resource "kubectl_manifest" "openshell_admin_sa_secret" {
  yaml_body = yamlencode({ apiVersion="v1", kind="Secret", metadata={name="openshell-admin-sa", namespace="openshell"},
    stringData={ OPENSHELL_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET = keycloak_openid_client.openshell_admin_sa.client_secret } })
  sensitive_fields = ["stringData.OPENSHELL_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET"]
}
 

F. The tools image — built in-cluster by kaniko, from a Dockerfile that lives in a ConfigMap

There's no CI job and no host Dockerfile here: the sandbox/terminal image (dev-toolbox-bash) is built inside the cluster by kaniko, and its Dockerfile is inline in a KRO ResourceGraphDefinition's ConfigMap.

👉So the whole image spec is GitOps'd as one CR.

Baking scripts → base64 one-liners.

Because the Dockerfile is a YAML string in a ConfigMap (no COPY from a build context), scripts are embedded as base64 blobs decoded at build time — byte-exact, single-line, no heredoc/escaping grief.

That's why the RUN lines look like this (the scoped-ops helper is ~8 KB of base64):

# the shell-init that auto-auths goose/claude to the in-cluster LiteLLM proxy + hydrates ~/.claude/skills:
RUN echo 'IyEvYmluL2Jhc2gK…（~3 KB base64…）' | base64 -d > /etc/profile.d/llm-clis.sh && chmod 0755 …
# the immersive scoped-ops helper (Appendix B), + auto-source its env on connect:
RUN echo 'IyEvdXNyL2Jpbi9lbnYgYmFzaAo…（~8 KB base64…）' | base64 -d > /usr/local/bin/scoped-ops && chmod 0755 …
RUN echo '[ -f /tmp/scoped-ops.env ] && . /tmp/scoped-ops.env' >> /etc/bash.bashrc
# the openshell CLI — PINNED (see "Honest edges"): the newest release with device-code but before the connect regression:
RUN curl -fsSL …/releases/download/v0.0.110/openshell-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz -o /tmp/o.tgz \
 && echo '<sha256>  /tmp/o.tgz' | sha256sum -c - && tar -xzf /tmp/o.tgz -C /tmp && install -m0755 …/openshell /usr/local/bin/
 

💡To edit a baked script: write it to a file, base64 -i f | tr -d '\n' > f.b64, verify it round-trips (base64 -D -i f.b64 | diff - f) and is charset-clean, then substitute the blob into the RUN line (use a tiny Python script — the blob is too big to hand-edit).

What's actually inside the first blob — llm-clis.sh (decoded).

This is the shell-init that makes goose and claude "just work" in a fresh terminal:

  • it reads the LiteLLM key from a Secret at runtime,
  • exports the provider env for both CLIs,
  • hydrates ~/.claude/skills from a ConfigMap,
  • and pre-clears Claude Code's first-run gates.

It's sourced from /etc/bash.bashrc, so every new shell gets it:

#!/bin/bash
# Busola terminal: auto-configure goose + Claude Code against the in-cluster litellm proxy, and hydrate
# ~/.claude/skills. The terminal pod is cluster-admin, so it can read the litellm master key + the skills ConfigMap.
_llm_env() {
  local key host
  export GOOSE_DISABLE_KEYRING=1   # no keyring/dbus in a container (goose reads the key from env)
  export GOOSE_TELEMETRY_OFF=1     # skip goose's first-run telemetry opt-in prompt
  key=$(kubectl get secret llm-proxy-credentials -n default -o jsonpath='{.data.PROXY_API_KEY}' 2>/dev/null | base64 -d 2>/dev/null)
  [ -n "$key" ] || return 0
  host=http://litellm-proxy.default.svc.cluster.local:4001
  # goose (OpenAI-compat /v1)
  export GOOSE_PROVIDER=litellm GOOSE_MODEL=anthropic--claude-4.6-sonnet
  export LITELLM_HOST="$host" LITELLM_API_KEY="$key"
  export OPENAI_BASE_URL="$host/v1" OPENAI_API_KEY="$key"
  # Claude Code (Anthropic-native /v1/messages). Use ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (sent as `Authorization: Bearer`, which
  # litellm's master-key accepts) — NOT ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (x-api-key), which the TUI rejects against a non-Anthropic URL.
  export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL="$host" ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN="$key"
  export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=anthropic--claude-4.7-opus ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL=anthropic--claude-4.5-sonnet
  # litellm model ids aren't in Claude Code's catalog → silence the unrecognized-model context-window warning.
  export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_UNKNOWN_MODEL_WINDOW_ENFORCEMENT=1
}
_skills_hydrate() {
  # Rehydrate ~/.claude/skills from the claude-skills ConfigMap (keys are path__with__double-underscores, base64 values).
  [ -d "$HOME/.claude/skills/bootstrapper" ] && return 0
  command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 0
  local json; json=$(kubectl get cm claude-skills -n default -o json 2>/dev/null) || return 0
  [ -n "$json" ] || return 0
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.claude/skills"
  printf '%s' "$json" | jq -r '.binaryData // {} | to_entries[] | .key + "\t" + .value' | while IFS=$'\t' read -r k v; do
    rel=${k//__//}
    mkdir -p "$HOME/.claude/skills/$(dirname "$rel")"
    printf '%s' "$v" | base64 -d > "$HOME/.claude/skills/$rel" 2>/dev/null
  done
}
_claude_onboarding() {
  # Skip Claude Code's first-run gates for this trusted cluster-admin terminal: mark onboarding complete, pre-allow
  # read-only diagnostics (so agentic runs don't prompt — --dangerously-skip-permissions is blocked as root), and
  # pre-trust the common working dirs so the "trust this folder?" dialog doesn't block the TUI.
  command -v jq >/dev/null 2>&1 || return 0
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.claude"
  [ -f "$HOME/.claude/settings.json" ] || printf '%s\n' \
    '{"permissions":{"allow":["Read","Glob","Grep","Bash(kubectl get:*)","Bash(kubectl describe:*)","Bash(kubectl logs:*)","Bash(kubectl top:*)","Bash(kyma:*)"]}}' \
    > "$HOME/.claude/settings.json"
  local f="$HOME/.claude.json" tmp
  [ -f "$f" ] || printf '{}' > "$f"
  jq -e '.hasCompletedOnboarding == true' "$f" >/dev/null 2>&1 && return 0
  tmp=$(mktemp) || return 0
  jq '. + {hasCompletedOnboarding:true, theme:(.theme // "dark")}
        | .projects = ((.projects // {}) + (["/root","/tmp",env.HOME] | map({(.):{hasTrustDialogAccepted:true}}) | add))' \
     "$f" > "$tmp" 2>/dev/null && mv "$tmp" "$f"
}
_goose_config() {
  # Seed goose's config.yaml so the interactive `goose session` skips its configure wizard (`goose run` already
  # works off the GOOSE_* env). The litellm key comes from LITELLM_API_KEY (GOOSE_DISABLE_KEYRING=1).
  local f="$HOME/.config/goose/config.yaml"
  [ -f "$f" ] && return 0
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.config/goose"
  printf 'GOOSE_PROVIDER: litellm\nGOOSE_MODEL: anthropic--claude-4.5-sonnet\n' > "$f"
}
_llm_env
_skills_hydrate
_claude_onboarding
_goose_config
 

Note the honest bit in the real file's comments (trimmed above for length): the interactive claude TUI shows a transient "streaming response ended … retrying" because the LiteLLM sap/ provider doesn't stream /v1/messages yet — headless claude -p + pipe are unaffected. The durable fix is streaming in the LiteLLM sap/ plugin.

Build vs. reach — two different addresses.

  • kaniko pushes to the registry's in-cluster Service DNS (dockerregistry.docker-registry.svc:5000, reachable from a pod).
  • Pods pull the same image via the registry's NodePort (localhost:32137/…:latest, imagePullPolicy: Always) — because the kubelet can't resolve cluster DNS for image pulls.
  • The tag is :latest (mutable), so a freshly-spawned terminal/sandbox re-pulls the new build automatically; existing sessions keep the old one.

Rebuilding (after editing the Dockerfile-in-the-RGD) is a small dance — apply the RGD so KRO re-renders the ConfigMap, then delete the completed build Job so KRO recreates it and kaniko rebuilds:

kubectl apply -f rgd-kaniko-devtoolbox.yaml          # KRO re-renders the <name>-dockerfile ConfigMap
kubectl -n image-build delete job kaniko-devtoolbox  # KRO recreates it → kaniko rebuilds + pushes
 
💡We codified exactly this into a repeatable runbook (a "rebuild-kaniko-image" skill) - so it's a push-button.

 🔧Troubleshooting

👉The ambushes that cost us real time, each with its fingerprint.

Keycloak / OIDC

  • HTTP 431 (Request Header Fields Too Large) on the first gRPC call — the access token is too big. Reusing a shared UI client with web_origins = ["+"] makes Keycloak reflect every valid redirect URI into a ~10 KB allowed-origins claim → a ~15 KB token → the OpenShell gateway's own HTTP/2 header limit rejects it (response_code_details: via_upstream pins the refusal to the gateway, not Envoy; a kubectl port-forward masks it by skipping Istio's x-forwarded-* headers). Fix: the dedicated openshell-oidc client with empty web_origins + just two loopback redirect URIs → a ~5 KB token that fits (Appendix E).
  • Device-code login 400s "Client is not allowed to initiate OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant" — the grant is OFF by default. Fix: oauth2_device_authorization_grant_enabled = true on the client.
  • The gateway rejects a token it should accept — Keycloak's access-token aud defaults to account, not your client, and the gateway checks server.oidc.audience against aud. Fix: the audience mapper so aud includes openshell-oidc (Appendix E).
  • The openshell-admin role never lands — two traps: use the advanced role IDP mapper (oidc-advanced-role-idp-mapper); the basic one can't match an array groups claim. And an IDP mapper only fires on a real broker login (redirect to the corp IdP), not an SSO-cookie re-auth — clear the session, then log in fresh.

The CLI, the gateway, and the image

  • connect hangs or attaches read-only — a CLI-version regression (a sandbox-lifecycle change in a later release altered how connect behaves). Fix: pin the CLI (we hold it a step behind the gateway; see "Honest edges").
  • subsystem request failed on channel 0 — you're connecting to a sandbox that's Completed/Error, not Ready. Fix: recreate the box; don't connect a stopped one.
  • Gateway pod stuck in ContainerCreating (MountVolume.SetUp failed) — the signing-key secret is missing. Fix: enable the PKI init job (pkiInitJob.enabled=true), which generates it (Appendix A).
  • terraform apply fails 409 "already exists" on the sandbox RBAC — an out-of-band kubectl-applied copy is squatting the name. Fix: delete the out-of-band objects, re-apply; Terraform then owns them.
  • A rebuilt image doesn't take effect — :latest is mutable and running pods keep their layer. Fix: open a fresh terminal / recreate the sandbox; to force the build itself, apply the RGD then delete the kaniko Job (Appendix F).
  • kyma alpha diagnose istio times out in the scoped-ops box — it reaches istiod/the sidecars directly, which the egress allow-list denies. Expected — apiserver-based diagnostics work; deep istio analysis is a web-terminal job.

📚References & links

Platform & tools — and the bill of materials (the exact versions we ran):

agent-sandboxv0.5.5github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandboxthe Kubernetes-SIG controller that turns a Sandbox CR into an isolated pod
Kubernetes (Gardener shoot)v1.35.7kubernetes.iothe shoot's node/control-plane version

kyma CLIv3 (alpha)github.com/kyma-project/cli

Kyma Istio module1.31.0-experimentalgithub.com/kyma-project/istio
Istio Module | SAP Help		manages the Istio install (the gateway's VirtualService rides it)
Kyma Telemetry module1.72.0github.com/kyma-project/telemetry-manager
Telemetry Module | SAP Help		logs/metrics/traces pipelines → SAP Cloud Logging

KeycloakKyma-deployedkeycloak.orgthe OIDC provider (device-code + PKCE)

OpenShell issues that shaped the deployment — ⚠️ pin against these:

 

Issue⚠️Why it matters here
⚠️#2726 — "canonical main process" (v0.0.111)changed connect behaviour → we floor the CLI at v0.0.110
⚠️#3648stale input-lease → read-only/unresponsive attach (open)
⚠️#3572subsystem request failed on channel 0 = connecting a Completed/Error sandbox
#2795device-code login (v0.0.110) — the browserless terminal path

📖Lexicon

TermWhat it means
Sandbox / agent-sandboxThe isolated pod the agent runs in, created from a Sandbox custom resource by the agent-sandbox controller. The pod, not a policy document, is the boundary — it has no usable network route except the supervisor.
SupervisorA process injected into every sandbox that owns the box's single exit. It intercepts all the agent's outbound traffic, enforces the allow-list, and injects the real LLM key at the last hop.
L7 allow-list (network policy)The supervisor's deny-by-default rule set: it names, at the application layer (L7), exactly which binary may reach which host:port over which protocol. Not to be confused with a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy (L3/L4).
Credential injection / placeholderThe trick that lets an agent call a paid model without ever holding the key: the agent sends a dummy x-api-key: placeholder; the supervisor swaps in the real key just before forwarding upstream. The key lives only in the gateway.
OIDCOpenID Connect, the standard login protocol. Here the gateway validates the OIDC token itself, so there's no separate login proxy in front of it.
Device-code flowThe browserless login: the CLI prints a URL + short code, you approve it on another device. Used from the web terminal, which has no browser of its own.
PKCEProof Key for Code Exchange — the extra handshake step that lets a "public" client (like a CLI, which can't keep a secret) log in securely.
gRPC / bidi (bidirectional) streamgRPC is Google's fast, binary RPC protocol (it rides HTTP/2). A bidi = bidirectional stream means both ends keep one long-lived connection open and send messages over it in both directions at once — like a phone call, not a letter-and-reply. openshell sandbox connect uses exactly this: your keystrokes stream up to the sandbox and its shell output streams down to you, continuously, over the same connection. Because that connection stays open for the whole session (not a quick request→response), the ingress in front of the gateway must impose no request/idle timeout or it would cut the shell mid-session.
GatewayThe single OpenShell pod that authenticates clients, holds the real LLM key, and drives the creation of sandboxes. Protect it and you protect everything.
KRO / ResourceGraphDefinition (RGD)A way to package a bundle of Kubernetes objects as one custom resource. We use it to ship the gateway's VirtualService, the one-time provider-setup Job, the sandbox reaper, and even the tools-image build recipe.
KanikoA tool that builds a container image inside the cluster (no Docker daemon, no external CI), so the whole image recipe can live in Git as one resource.
Scoped-opsOur middle trust tier: a sandbox that additionally gets a short-lived, read-only cluster credential so an agent can inspect the cluster and reason about it — but never change it, never read secrets, never reach the internet.

Written from a real deployment on a SAP Kyma TechEd fleet. OpenShell is NVIDIA's Apache-2.0 sandboxed-agent runtime; agent-sandbox is a Kubernetes-SIG project. Nothing here requires a fork — it's the stock chart, wired to SAP AI Core.

entry.title: SAP Integration Suite at SAP TechEd 2026: Let’s Meet in Berlin!
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community,

entry.title: Terraform@SAP TechEd Berlin 2026: Define, Generate, Deploy – AI-Driven Spec-First Terraform | XP265
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP TechEd is back in Berlin — October 27–29, 2026 at Messe Berlin — and this year's agenda of course circles around agentic AI. Thinking about platform automation, where can AI adds value with the tasks you are facing when trying to automate the setup of the platform for your development teams via Terraform?

We will give our answer to that in the hands-on session XP265 | Define, generate, deploy: AI-driven spec-first Terraform.

 

What This Session Is About

Terraform has become the standard language for infrastructure automation to provision and manage resources on the platform like subaccounts, entitlements and service instances. As of today, your Terraform code is probably hand-crafted or you are using AI to help with creating the code.

In the latter case you probably paste in prompts into an AI tool and reiterate until the code works. And let’s be honest, you probably forget the prompts that led you to the result you provisioned to prod (I have been there)

This leaves a lot of promises behind that come with Terraform like collaborative work, enabling governance and secure as well as compliant setup.  

In the hands-on session XP265 you will experience a different approach that overcomes these drawbacks.

Spec-driven Development

The main idea is to define a specification (or to be precise several specification documents) that capture your intent in detail and store it as markdown files that can be re-iterated upon and reused in other setups like the governance constraints you have in your organization.

One further ingredient of this approach is that we support with skills for the AI tool that give you guidance and have the good practices for the setup baked in.

In contrast to free-style prompting you can use our skill as commands in the agentic tool of your choice and follow along a structured flow from setting up the governance constraints to defining and detailing your scenario to generating Terraform Code.

What will be part of the hands-on workshop

You will experience the spec-driven development flow from start to end namely:

  • Do the basic setup of the tooling
  • Initialize the project via the spec-kit
  • Define the governance constraints
  • Define the scenario
  • Detail the account setup
  • Detail the service setup
  • Detail the security setup
  • Detail the connectivity setup
  • Define the tasks
  • Evaluate the design
  • Generate the Terraform code
  • Deploy the generated Terraform code

The foundation for this is “Infrastructure-as-Code Specification Toolkit for SAP Business AI Platform” that is available as open source at https://github.com/SAP/iac-spec-kit-for-sap-business-ai-platform

Who Should Attend

XP265 is aimed at administrators, platform engineers, and architects who are responsible for automating their platform setup. You need to be familiar with BTP concepts like subaccounts, entitlements, directories, etc. Basic Terraform knowledge is not required, but of course an advantage.

If you are already using Terraform provider and are curious about this approach this session will give you some inspiration on how to deal with Terraform and agentic AI.

How to sign up and/or get in touch

Check the session catalog for XP265, and sign up (places are limited)

I am looking forward seeing you in the session!

P.S. If you are at TechEd and want to get in touch with me to talk about Terraform and Platform automation (and don’t want to attend the hands-on), just drop me a line on LinkedIn – happy to have a chat

entry.title: Teched2026-XP266 -- Ship your own sandboxed AI operations agent to Kyma in two hours
entry.content:
Bring your own agent to a contained SAP Kyma sandbox with OpenRouter

Plug OpenRouter - a public LLM aggregator - into a contained sandbox with three off-the-shelf coding agents powered by free NVIDIA Nemotron models

This is a follow-up to Teched2026-XP266 | Giving an AI agent a shell — without giving away the keys to your cluster.
That post built the contained sandbox on SAP Kyma: the box is the boundary, three trust tiers, and an agent that reasons through a frontier model it never holds the key to.
Here we add a fourth tier — an external provider — and run somebody else's coding agents on a free public model, without loosening a single guarantee.

TL;DR

  • The sandbox model generalizes. "The in-cluster LLM proxy" was never special — it was just one provider. Swap in OpenRouter (a public aggregator) and the box behaves identically: one allow-listed host, nothing else.
  • Bring the model, not the key. The real OpenRouter key lives only in the gateway. Inside the box the agent carries a sentinel; the supervisor swaps it for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary → a listed host.
  • Three off-the-shelf agents, one image, a free model. opencode, Pi, and Qwen Code — all pointed at free NVIDIA Nemotron models on OpenRouter.
  • Containment holds with a public host in the mix. The box reaches openrouter.ai and nothing else — not the internet at large, not the API server. We prove it with three curls.
  • "External" isn't "less contained." Opening one host for named binaries, with the key injected at the wire, is a different tier — not a looser one.
  • The abstraction was the product. The sandbox never cared whether the model was in-cluster or across the planet; "provider" is the seam, and it holds.
  • A free model is a confident junior. Great for a first draft, wrong about anything niche — so make the cluster the reviewer, not the reader.

Contents

  • ⚖️ The itch
  • 🧭 The fourth tier
  • 👀 See it first
  • 🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox
  • 🔍 The deep dive
    • 3a. The profile is the policy
    • 3b. The provider holds the key
    • 3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel
    • 3d. Picking a free model
  • ️🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix
  • 🎯 Why it's worth it
  • 🧰 Reusable patterns
  • 📎 Appendix
  • 📚 References & BOM
  • 📖 Lexicon
  • 🎓 See it live — SAP TechEd 2026 (XP266)

⚖️ The itch — one more model, one more key

👉The first post left the agent talking to SAP AI Core, in-cluster, through an in-cluster LLM proxy — no key in the box, no route to the internet.

👉However, sooner or later someone will need a feature the in-cluster proxy doesn't bridge yet, for instance:

  • a public aggregator,
  • a shiny free model to prototype with,
  • an off-the-shelf coding agent that only knows how to talk to OpenRouter.

👉So the question remains:

How do you let an agent use an external model — reached over the public internet — without putting the key in the box or opening a route it can abuse?

👉The answer turns out to be not a new mechanism at all.

🧭 The fourth tier — an external provider

The first post had three tiers — the same sandbox image, with each tier granting a bit more access - the more you trust the workload. 

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
1. Containedthe in-cluster LLM onlynonenone (sentinel)
2. Scoped-ops+ API server (read-only)read-only kubectlnone (sentinel)
3. Web terminalfull pod networkRBAC-scoped kubectlnone (sentinel)

This external provider adds a fourth tier — same pattern adding one more row:

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
4. External agentone public host (openrouter.ai)nonenone (sentinel)

👉And it is not a weaker tier — it's a different one.

  • The box still can't reach the API server or the rest of the internet. 
  • And the only thing that changed is which single endpoint the supervisor opens, and that the credential behind it is a real OpenRouter key — held, as always, by the gateway and never by the box.

👀 See it first — from the web terminal

  • Kyma web terminal embeds the openshell CLI
  • the terminal runs inside the cluster, thus, you reach the gateway's Service directly (no HTTPS host, no port-forward).
  • The openshell gateway is OIDC-gated; it validates your Keycloak token itself.
  • The terminal has no browser, so you log in with the device-code flow:

 

export XP266_CLUSTER=xp266-NNN          # your runtime number
export XP266_DOMAIN=<workshop-domain>   # handed out at the session

OPENSHELL_NO_BROWSER=1 openshell gateway add http://openshell.openshell.svc.cluster.local:8080 \
  --oidc-issuer https://keycloak.$XP266_CLUSTER.$XP266_DOMAIN/realms/ateam-isveng \
  --oidc-client-id openshell-oidc
#   To authenticate, visit:
#     https://keycloak.<cluster>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng/device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX
#   ✓ Authenticated via device code      ← approve on your laptop, you need the `openshell-admin` role

👉pick a current free model and create the sandbox:

 

export FREE_MODEL=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free   # a current :free NVIDIA model

openshell sandbox create --name agents \
  --from localhost:32137/openrouter-agents:latest \
  --provider openrouter \
  --env OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 \
  --env OPENAI_MODEL=$FREE_MODEL \
  --detach -- sleep infinity &
openshell sandbox list        # wait for PHASE=Ready
👉--provider openrouter is the whole trick: it opens egress to openrouter.ai (+ models.dev) for the agent binaries only, and injects the key sentinel.

👉Run any of the three agents — same box, same model:

# opencode (open-source Bun agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- opencode run -m openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "Reply with one word: PONG"
#   PONG

# Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- pi -p --model openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "List 3 facts about Kyma."

# Qwen Code (OpenAI-compatible — takes no -m; reads $OPENAI_MODEL):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- qwen -p "List 3 facts about Kyma."
 

👉An off-the-shelf coding agent just reasoned through a frontier-grade free model.

Now the punchline: try to break out

openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- sh -c '
  curl -sS -m8 -o /dev/null -w "openrouter.ai: %{http_code}\n" https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models
  curl -sS -m8 https://example.com            >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "example.com: REACHED" || echo "example.com: blocked"
  curl -sS -m8 https://kubernetes.default.svc >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "apiserver: REACHED"   || echo "apiserver: blocked"
  echo "key in box: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
 
openrouter.ai: 200
example.com: blocked                     ← the rest of the internet: no route
apiserver: blocked                       ← the cluster API: no route
key in box: openshell:resolve:env:…      ← a sentinel, NOT the real key

👉One host reachable.

  • ✅Everything else refused.
  • ✅The key never in the box.
  • ✅That's the fourth tier in three curl lines.

🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox

Three concepts, one key that never leaves the gateway:

  • Profile — a reusable spec, no secret in it: which credential env var, which auth style, which endpoints egress may reach, and which binaries are allowed to use the credential.
  • Provider — a profile bound to a real key. The key (sk-or-…) is stored only in the gateway.
  • Sandbox — --provider openrouter attaches it: the box receives a sentinel (not the key) + scoped egress; the supervisor swaps the sentinel for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary reaching a listed endpoint.
 

 

Same picture, in ASCII, for renderers that don't do Mermaid:

   ┌───────────────── OpenShell gateway (holds the real key) ───────────────── ┐
   │ profile "openrouter"   credential: OPENROUTER_API_KEY (bearer)            │
   │                        endpoints : openrouter.ai, models.dev  ← only hosts│
   │                        binaries  : node, opencode, qwen, pi   ← only these│
   │ provider "openrouter" = profile + REAL KEY           ← key lives ONLY here│
   └───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                 sandbox create --provider openrouter
                                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── your sandbox (the box) ────────────────────┐
   │ OPENROUTER_API_KEY = openshell:resolve:…   ← a SENTINEL        │
   │ agent  ──▶  Authorization: Bearer <sentinel>                   │
   └───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                        ▼ (allowed binary + allowed host)
            supervisor swaps  <sentinel> → sk-or-…  AT THE WIRE
                                        ▼
                                  openrouter.ai   (sees the real key; the box never did)
 
In a nutshell:
  • 👉The gateway is the keeper of secrets
  • 👉the profile is the policy
  • 👉the sentinel is what the agent gets instead of a key.

🔍 The deep dive

3a. The profile is the policy (endpoints × binaries)

  • A profile answers two questions and nothing else: which hosts may this credential reach, and which binaries may send that traffic.
  • For OpenRouter that's openrouter.ai (the inference API) plus models.dev (opencode's model-registry metadata, dialed on startup), and the agent binaries (node, opencode, qwen, pi).
  • Everything outside that cross product is denied by default — a block-list would be a guessing game; an allow-list is a decision you can read.

3b. The provider holds the key — once, in one place

  • The provider is the profile plus a real key.
  • On OpenShell 0.1.1 the key is injected into the box as a resolve-sentinel (openshell:resolve:env:…); the supervisor resolves it to the real sk-or-… only at egress, and only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.
  • The two env vars the agents read — OPENROUTER_API_KEY (Pi, opencode) and OPENAI_API_KEY (the OpenAI-compatible Qwen Code) — both carry the sentinel.
  • Compromise the agent and all you've got is the string openshell:resolve:env:….

3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel, never the secret

  • This is the same credential-injection trick from the first post, now across a public hop instead of an in-cluster one.
  • The box's view of the world: an env var that looks like a key but isn't, and exactly one host it's allowed to send it to.
  • The agent can't tell the difference — it sets Authorization: Bearer <sentinel> and the reply comes back — but an attacker who owns the agent gets a placeholder and a single, logged, allow-listed destination.

3d. Picking a free model

OpenRouter's :free tier includes NVIDIA's Nemotron family — frontier-grade, no quota spent.

  • The agents call tools, so the model must be a chat/completion model with tool-calling. Embedding/rerank models (ids with -embed- / -rerank-) are RAG parts, not chat — the agent will error.
  • Two known-good picks: nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free (large, higher quality) and nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free (smaller, faster).

🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix

  • 👉 The instinct is that "the box can now reach the internet" must mean "the box is less safe."
  • 👉 It doesn't — because the internet was never opened.

Here's what each familiar threat runs into:

ThreatWhat usually enables itWhat this tier does instead
Data exfiltrationthe agent has the internetone host resolves (openrouter.ai); example.com and everything else → no route
Reaching the clusterpod → API server pathno route to kubernetes.default.svc — this tier grants no cluster access at all
Credential theftthe agent holds the keythe key is never in the box — a sentinel in, the real sk-or-… injected at the last hop
A rogue binary phoning homeany process can egressegress is binary-scoped — only node/opencode/qwen/pi may send; anything else is denied
Silent abuseno audit trailevery denied request is logged at the supervisor

 

 

🎯 Why it's worth it

You can say yes to a much wider set of "can the agent use this model?" questions, because "use" now happens somewhere it can't hurt you — even when the model lives on the public internet behind a paid key:

  • ✅ off-the-shelf coding agents (opencode, Pi, Qwen Code) you didn't write and don't fully trust, run safely
  • ✅ free models for prototyping and workshops — no quota, no standing credential in the box
  • ✅ the same contained guarantees as the in-cluster tier: one host, no cluster, key in the gateway
  • ✅ a clean generalization — "provider" means any governed endpoint, in-cluster or external, by the same rules

All on the stock OpenShell chart and agent-sandbox controller, on a normal managed Kyma cluster.

🧰 Reusable patterns

Strip out OpenRouter and several of these stand on their own — a toolkit for governing any external dependency a semi-trusted workload needs.

  • Model the credential as a profile, not an env var. Separate the spec (which hosts, which binaries, which auth) from the secret. The spec is reviewable in Git; the secret lives in exactly one guarded place. ✅ You can audit "what can reach the internet" without ever seeing a key.
  •  Scope egress by binary, not just by host. "node and opencode may reach openrouter.ai" is a far tighter statement than "the pod may reach openrouter.ai." A rogue process in the box still can't send. ✅ Lateral egress inside the box is closed, not just lateral network.
  • Inject credentials at the wire — even across a public hop. The workload carries a sentinel; the proxy swaps in the real value on the last hop out. Works identically whether the destination is in-cluster or on the internet. ✅ Compromise the workload and the attacker gets the word "placeholder".
  • One proxy, two shapes. OpenAI-compatible gateways (SAP AI Core, OpenRouter) look the same to a proxy — so one in-cluster exit can front both, spend-tracked, keys never leaving it. ✅ Add a provider without adding an egress path.
  • Free tiers make experimentation cheap — pin against their churn. A :free model is perfect for a workshop or a spike; its instability is the price. Keep a fallback and list-before-you-run. ✅ Zero-cost iteration, with a documented escape hatch when a model goes paid.
  • Let the platform adjudicate generated code. For anything an LLM writes against a niche API, make the API server the gate: --dry-run=server before trust. The draft→reject→fix loop is the workflow. ✅ The model's confidence stops mattering; the cluster's acceptance is the only verdict.

👉The recipe, in one line:

credential-as-profile → binary-scoped egress → sentinel-at-the-wire → one proxy, two shapes → free tier with a fallback → the cluster adjudicates generated code.

📎 Appendix

 

A. The provider profile (what --provider openrouter binds to)

Wired once per gateway (the real key is handed to the gateway here and never leaves it):

  • The profile lists the endpoints egress may reach (openrouter.ai, models.dev) and the binaries allowed to use the credential; the provider is that profile plus the real sk-or-….
  • Inside the box the agents see only the sentinel in OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY;
  • The supervisor resolves it at egress for an allowed binary → an allowed host.

The profile itself (imported into the gateway) — the whole policy is the endpoint × binary cross-product:

 

id: openrouter
display_name: OpenRouter
inference_capable: true
credentials:
  - name: api_key
    env_vars: [OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY]   # agents read either; injected as a resolve-sentinel, swapped at egress
    auth_style: bearer
    header_name: authorization
endpoints:
  - { host: openrouter.ai, port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-write }   # the inference API (/api/v1/…)
  - { host: models.dev,    port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-only }    # opencode's model registry (dialed on startup)
binaries:
  - /usr/local/bin/node                                        # Pi + Qwen Code — the connecting process is node
  - /usr/local/bin/opencode                                    # opencode launcher symlink
  - /usr/local/lib/node_modules/opencode-ai/bin/opencode.exe   # opencode's RESOLVED Bun ELF (the symlink alone fails)

Why both OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY?

👉 Because the three agents expect the key under different env-var names, and listing both makes the gateway inject the sentinel under each — so whichever name an agent reads, it finds it:

  • OPENROUTER_API_KEY → Pi and opencode (OpenRouter-native).
  • OPENAI_API_KEY → Qwen Code, which is an OpenAI-compatible client and reads the OpenAI name.

Binding the real key turns the profile into a provider: 

The key is read from an in-cluster Secret and handed to the gateway once — it is stored only there, and every sandbox created --provider openrouter receives the sentinel, never the key.

(No tls: on the endpoints — the supervisor terminates TLS transparently and injects a CA bundle: CURL_CA_BUNDLE / NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.)

 

B. The tools image — built in-cluster by kaniko

openrouter-agents:latest is built inside the cluster by kaniko (no CI, no registry credentials), from a Dockerfile that lives inline in a ConfigMap.

The three agents are the whole payload:

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim
# bash + CA certs for TLS to openrouter.ai; fd + ripgrep pre-installed so the agents' search tools work WITHOUT
# sandbox-blocked downloads; git for repo awareness; curl.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      bash ca-certificates fd-find git ripgrep curl \
 && ln -s /usr/bin/fdfind /usr/local/bin/fd && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# Pi + Qwen Code — pure-JS, installed with --ignore-scripts (supply-chain hygiene, no postinstall):
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@latest"
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@qwen-code/qwen-code@latest"
# opencode — postinstall ALLOWED so it fetches the correct glibc platform binary for this base → /usr/local/bin/opencode:
RUN npm install -g --allow-scripts=opencode-ai "opencode-ai@latest"
# OpenShell 0.1.x runs the sandbox as uid 10001: add a passwd entry so $USER/$HOME resolve + a writable home:
RUN echo 'agent:x:10001:0:agent sandbox:/home/agent:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd \
 && mkdir -p /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent && chmod -R 0777 /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent
WORKDIR /home/agent
ENV PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=/tmp/pi-agent
 

C. OpenRouter vs SAP AI Core — the same shape

Why does an external provider slot in so cleanly?

  • Because OpenRouter and SAP AI Core are the same shape to a proxy: an OpenAI-compatible gateway behind one credential.
  • OpenRouter is a public aggregator (one endpoint, many upstreams — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Qwen, NVIDIA…)
  • SAP AI Core is SAP's managed inference gateway, reached in-cluster through a proxy.

So OpenRouter is just another provider — no new integration, the same sentinel-at-the-wire mechanism.

 SAP AI Core (via in-cluster LLM proxy)OpenRouter (via direct path)
Pathagent → in-cluster proxy → SAP AI Coreagent → OpenRouter (one allow-listed external host)
Key in boxnone — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)none — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)
Internetnoneone host: openrouter.ai

In summary:

  • 👉The key story is identical — in both, the real credential lives only in the gateway and the box carries a sentinel.
  • 👉The only things that differ are the egress path (an in-cluster service vs one public host) and whether any internet is opened at all.
  • ⚠️The one thing that does not work: OpenRouter cannot call SAP AI Core. OpenRouter only routes to its own public upstreams — it can't reach an in-cluster proxy.

📚References & BOM

The exact versions this ran on a managed SAP Kyma TechEd fleet:

NVIDIA OpenShell0.1.1 (gateway chart + CLI)github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShellApache-2.0; beta. 0.1.x retired inference.local → direct proxy dial + resolve-sentinel
agent-sandboxv0.5.5github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandboxthe controller turning a Sandbox CR into an isolated pod
OpenRouterpublic aggregatoropenrouter.aione OpenAI-compatible endpoint + one key → many upstreams
NVIDIA Nemotron (:free)rotatingopenrouter.ai/models?max_price=0&q=nvidiatool-calling chat models

entry.title: [SAP TechEd Berlin - BT161 + BT160] Two workshops, one goal: put AI under control.
entry.content:
AI is spreading through organizations faster than anyone can track. AI agents you didn't approve. Applications nobody fully owns anymore. Decisions made in people's heads, not on paper.
 
At TechEd 2026 Berlin, we're running two hands-on workshops that put you in the architect's seat and let you experience what it actually looks like to govern AI — with real tools, a real scenario, and a real outcome at the end.
 
No slides. No demos. You do the work.

BT161 — From Discovery to Decommissioning: A Hands-On AI Governance Workshop

 
The scenario: GlobalFlex AG just got an audit finding. No central inventory of AI agents exists, and several are touching sensitive data without any risk assessment. The CIO has given the EA team 90 days to fix it. That EA team is you.
 
Over six exercises learn how the SAP AI Agent Hub supports the full governance lifecycle of existing and newly discovered agents:
  1. Use the EA Assistant to draft an Architecture Decision Record for the governance policy your committee just adopted — AI does the writing, you do the governing
  2. Spot the new agent in the discovery inbox and pull it into your governed inventory
  3. Complete the governance profile — link the ADR you just created, assign ownership
  4. Use the EA Assistant to send a survey to the agent's business owner for the fields you're missing — AI risk level, model, owner — and actually wait for the response before you can proceed
  5. Verify the agent once the full record is in place
  6. Decommission a legacy agent, link its successor, close its lifecycle
    It's the complete arc — from "something showed up" to "this is fully governed" — in less than 120 minutes.
     
    No prior SAP LeanIX experience needed. No coding. Just curiosity and a need for governance.
    Register for BT161
     

    BT160 — Govern with Enterprise Architecture Assistant and MCP


    The scenario: InDAC runs business-process outsourcing for insurance and telco clients. Its core platform — MaMa-CRM — was built in-house, runs the whole business, and is the system nobody fully owns anymore. The Board wants a formal review with evidence before deciding whether to keep it, re-platform it, or retire it. Jack, the CIO, just put it on your desk.
    This workshop uses two surfaces into the same LeanIX workspace:
    • Claude Code connected via the LeanIX MCP server — to create a governed Architecture Decision Record straight from your terminal

The EA Assistant — to explore the application's landscape, run an evidence-based review against a formal standard, and check for EU AI Act exposure

By the end, you'll hand the Board a defensible keep / re-platform / retire verdict — built from actual architecture data, live web research, and your own analysis.
No prior SAP LeanIX or MCP experience needed. (You'll use Claude Code briefly, but everything is set up for you.)
Register for BT160
 

How they pair together

 
These workshops sit in different subtracks, but they're two sides of the same coin:

BT160 is about the applications and architecture — reviewing what you have, with AI as your co-analyst

Both use SAP LeanIX as the single source of truth. Both let you experience AI-native EA in practice, not in theory.
If you have time for one: pick the one that matches your role. If you have time for both: do BT160 in the morning and BT161 in the afternoon. You'll leave SAP TechEd with a complete picture of what modern EA governance looks like.
